title: Ida Cox, Skinny, and pianists who could not read music
summary: Talk of Ida Cox and a self-taught pianist called Skinny leads to the interviewer's remarks on great New Orleans and Texas pianists of the 1920s-30s who could not read.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Oh yeah. Well when I left there I left there with Ida Cox.

Incidentally I see where she gotta write up where she stuff Yeah, she cut out and cut some records again. I'd like to hear that. I played for her. And that little boy out of Houston, I don't know if you remember him, dog, my name was Skinny, he couldn't read but he could play the best piano player ever in my life. He was really terrific.

Well it seemed in those days, I'll say from the early 20s to the first to the 30s, most of the piano players, they didn't read. You take in New Orleans, Paul, there were a number of piano players while they couldn't read but played so terrific piano.
And the chords were perfect. You can check them today and the chords were right, it was great.

The guy that left here, Edgar Perry, call him Edgar, Edgar Perry. He had a tremendous, a royal garden band. Royal garden band. Edgar Perry, he was a terrific pianist. I couldn't read a note. No. And so many others. I mean I could name the fellas that I knew around at it, terrific musicians that couldn't read. Well you take for instance the pianist that Pihon had so long, Steve Lewis. Well Steve was, I imagine you recall some of his recordings if you heard them. Well Steve was sincere. I just heard it. He was sincere. Yeah.
